options.title: The Bleach Wash That Saved Vienna
options.description:
In 1847, Dr. Ignaz Semmelweis realized doctors were carrying unseen contaminants from autopsies into delivery rooms. By enforcing chlorinated lime handwashing, hospital death rates plummeted.

Sources:
- Semmelweis, I. (1861). The Etiology, Concept, and Prophylaxis of Childbed Fever.
- Loudon, I. (2000). The Tragedy of Childbed Fever.
script_lines: In 1847, a young Hungarian doctor forced every surgeon in Vienna to scrub their hands in chloride solution before delivering babies.
Vienna General Hospital was losing thousands of mothers, and doctors frequently walked directly from performing autopsies straight to the maternity ward.
The senior chief mocked the idea, muttering, "Gentlemen are inherently clean, Ignaz, and water changes nothing."
Semmelweis just pointed to the wash basins and replied, "Scrub them anyway."
Senior staff resisted, but within weeks, maternal mortality in the doctor's ward plummeted from eighteen percent down to under two.
Tiny cadaverous particles were hitching a ride on unwashed fingers, acting like muddy boots tracking dirt onto clean carpet.
Outbreak rates subsided, proving why a simple basin of lime wash transformed modern medicine.

options.title: The Glass Sphere That Ended Surgical Pain
options.description:
In 1846, dentist William Morton demonstrated ether anesthesia at Massachusetts General Hospital, turning surgical procedures from terrifying pain into quiet slumber.

Sources:
- Fenster, J. M. (2001). Ether Day: The Strange Tale of America's Greatest Medical Discovery.
- Massachusetts General Hospital Archives (1846).
script_lines: In 1846, a young dentist walked into a crowded Boston operating theater carrying a round glass globe filled with sweet ether gas.
Before that morning, surgery was a terrifying nightmare of screaming patients held down by four strong men.
The chief surgeon eyed the strange glass apparatus skeptically, warning, "Your odd trick will only suffocate the poor boy."
Morton adjusted the brass valve, held out the glass nozzle, and calmly whispered, "Just let him breathe."
The patient drifted into a deep sleep, and the surgeon removed a tumor while the room watched in dead silence.
Ether molecules blocked sensory signals in the brain, working like a temporary circuit breaker on the nervous system.
The patient woke asking when the cut would start, proving how a glass globe changed medicine forever.

options.title: The Carpenter's Watch That Saved Ships
options.description:
In 1761, John Harrison tested his marine chronometer H4 on a transatlantic voyage to Jamaica, solving the long-standing longitude problem.

Sources:
- Sobel, D. (1995). Longitude: The True Story of a Lone Genius Who Solved the Greatest Scientific Problem of His Time.
- National Maritime Museum Greenwich Archives.
script_lines: In 1761, a stubborn carpenter boarded a British warship holding a five-inch silver pocket watch he spent thirteen years building.
The Royal Navy was losing fleets to shipwreck because sailors had no accurate way to calculate longitude across open ocean.
Astronomers laughed at the contraption, boasting, "No delicate clock can survive ocean storms; only the stars tell real time!"
Harrison tapped the silver casing and answered, "My springs keep time where your stars are hidden by clouds."
After an eighty-one day voyage across the Atlantic, his watch was off by less than five seconds.
Knowing precise London time let sailors compare local sun position, like checking two cell phones set to different time zones.
Shipwreck risks subsided across the fleet, all because a carpenter put a watch on a ship.
